A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. All 17 pages of v2 and 18 pages of v3, including appendices, are readable, and their methods, tables, equations, and figures can be reliably matched.

before.justification: V2 reports original experiments on direct and indirect prompt injection, model utility, efficiency, attack transfer, and defense comparisons.

after.justification: V3 retains original defense experiments and reports additional AutoDAN, sentiment-classification, instruction-deletion, and retrieved-data-removal results.

M1.justification: The four defense constructions in Section 4 remain unchanged. V3 Section 5.4 adds a proposed adaptation for long instructions: truncate the leading instruction while retaining its repetition in the final defense prompt. Instruction-deletion experiments test this optional prompting modification.

E1.justification: V3 adds explicit SST2 sentiment-classification utility evaluation, supplementing the retained AlpacaFarm and QA coverage. Its long-instruction discussion does not introduce an actual long-query benchmark; the deletion experiments use existing benchmarks.

E2.justification: V3 adds AutoDAN, attributed to Zhu et al. (2023), as an evaluated attack against the defenses in Table 4. GCG remains evaluated. The five training-free defense baselines and StruQ variants retain their membership in the corresponding retained comparisons.

E3.justification: V3 adds controls deleting the leading instruction on Llama3 and removing retrieved QA data. Table 9 explicitly retains an undeleted, undefended input as the None control. It drops the Llama3-to-Llama3.1 GCG-transfer evaluation and seconds-per-item efficiency measurement. The main sample counts, ASR/accuracy metrics, and generation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The supplementary analysis suite changes substantially. V3 adds instruction-deletion tests for attack resistance and QA utility (Tables 8–9), plus a retrieved-data-removal ablation (Appendix A.3, Table 11). It adds AutoDAN defense testing but removes GCG transfer analysis and the efficiency study. The attack-strength relationship, template-attack analysis, and response case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, uncertainty bars, or statistical significance tests. Figure 3 retains averages across attack or defense methods, without uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: V3 retains the Llama3 GCG scores but replaces the Llama3.1 transfer column with Llama3 AutoDAN results: 68.75% ASR without defense and 10.57% with Ours-Fakecom-t. These are different experimental conditions. Tables 8–11 add instruction-deletion, SST2, and no-retrieval results, while timing results disappear. The matched original benchmark tables and all figure results retain their values.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 retains the same mathematical formulation of clean inference, injection, and shield-prompt defense. No definitions, derivations, theorems, or proofs are added or revised. V3's acknowledgment that a mathematical explanation is absent changes the limitations discussion.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the claims that attack techniques inspire effective training-free defenses, outperform baselines, and sometimes reduce ASR to zero. V3 explicitly names prompt-engineering and gradient-based attacks in the introduction, but v2 already evaluated and claimed effectiveness against both.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive discussion of context-window overflow, deletion as an imperfect proxy for long queries, dependence on retrieved data, and the absence of mathematical justification. It replaces v2's expectation of stronger gradient-derived defenses with an assertion that prior performance was unsatisfactory. It also drops the speculative explanation of Qwen2's vulnerability and replaces the GCG suffix-transfer discussion with interpretation of defense generalization across attacks.

D1.justification: V3 newly states that only the attack technique used to construct a defense is assumed known. It removes v2's description of following Chen et al.'s GCG implementation with conversation-template knowledge, along with runtime information. The PyTorch version, A100 hardware, generation settings, dataset-access statements, and promised code release are unchanged.

R1.justification: V3 adds Socher et al. (2013) for SST2 and Zhu et al. (2023) for AutoDAN. Section 2 and the central positioning of repurposing attacks as defenses remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Editing is localized to evaluation passages and the rewritten limitations. V3 removes Model Efficiency, reorders the implementation and baseline appendix subsections, adds a data-removal subsection, and unnumbers Limitations and Ethical Consideration. The abstract, method exposition, and overall narrative structure remain largely intact.

P2.justification: V3 substantially reorganizes experimental displays: it adds Tables 8–11, removes the timing table, and changes the gradient table's columns from victim models to attack methods. The closed-source comparison moves to the appendix and StruQ moves into the main text. Captions explicitly identify metrics. All sixteen figures retain their graphics, with placement and appendix grouping changed.

improvement.justification: V3 modestly strengthens applicability assessment: SST2 extends utility testing beyond QA, AutoDAN tests another attack method, and the data-removal ablation shows the utility cost of discarding retrieved evidence. It also acknowledges that instruction deletion only approximates long-query handling. These benefits are tempered by removal of timing and cross-model GCG-transfer evidence; the central methods and retained results are stable.
